case_study_insert.main_stem: Kelvin Valve and Pump (KVP) is a public limited company in the industrial equipment sector, employing a workforce of 120. Founded in 1998 by Danica Kelvin, it supplies control valves to water utilities and operates a flat structure with democratic leadership. KVP plans to invest $1,200,000 in an automated valve-testing line, financed by a $700,000 five-year bank loan and a $500,000 share issue. It has fixed costs of $450,000 a year, a variable cost of $11.00 a unit and a selling price of $20.00, and produces 100,000 units a year. KVP faces two problems: absenteeism has reached 8% and the defect rate on cast valve bodies is rising at its Stoke foundry, delaying deliveries.
case_study_insert.appendix_1_marketing_ops: Quality and Waste Report — March 2025: The valve-testing line completed 25,000 units last month, with a defect rate of 3.1% on cast bodies, down from 4.0% in December. Customer complaints fell from 52 to 29 a month. Average delivery time is 8.2 days. A survey of 350 water-utility purchasing officers found 61% require a pressure-test certificate and 44% had delayed an order because of late delivery; 12 of 120 workers took unplanned leave exceeding nine days last month, and agency cover costs $230 a day.

case_study_insert.appendix_3_external_environment: Economic and Business Bulletin (February 2026): (1) The central bank cut the base interest rate from 5.0% to 4.25%, lowering borrowing costs on variable-rate loans. (2) The national minimum wage will rise by 5.8% from $12.80 to $13.54 per hour from April 2026. (3) Wholesale iron and bronze prices have risen 11.0% year-on-year, while manufacturing input inflation is 5.5% and water-utility capital spending is forecast to rise 3.2%.

questions.question_text: KVP is funding its $1,200,000 valve-testing line with a $700,000 bank loan and a $500,000 share issue. Explain two advantages for KVP of using a share issue rather than the bank loan.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Share capital does not have to be repaid and dividends can be paid only when profits allow, unlike the fixed interest and instalments on a $700,000 five-year bank loan. As a public limited company KVP can issue shares to investors, so the $500,000 raised strengthens the balance sheet without adding to the $450,000 annual fixed costs. This matters while the defect rate on cast bodies is still 3.1% and output of 100,000 units has to be maintained.

Point 2: Equity finance avoids the collateral and covenants a lender would demand, leaving KVP's existing assets free and its flat structure of democratic leadership unencumbered by lender conditions. With a workforce of 120 and absenteeism at 8%, the firm needs flexibility to spend on agency cover at $230 a day rather than commit cash to debt service. A share issue also spreads the risk of the $1,200,000 testing line across shareholders instead of leaving Danica Kelvin's management exposed to a single bank.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid point identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual explanation and analysis applied to KVP.

questions.question_text: KVP is tendering for new control-valve contracts. Consider trade-directory advertising, an industry exhibition, or direct mail to utility procurement teams. Which should KVP choose to win contracts? Justify your recommendation.
questions.model_answer:
Trade-directory advertising: Listing in a water-industry directory gives KVP a permanent, low-cost presence where purchasing officers search for suppliers. It reaches many potential buyers, but a small entry cannot demonstrate that 61% of the 350 surveyed officers require a pressure-test certificate, and it does not tackle the 8.2-day delivery time that has already caused 44% to delay orders. For a firm with $450,000 fixed costs, such passive exposure converts slowly.

Industry exhibition: A stand allows KVP to display valves and issue test certificates face to face, which suits buyers who demand proof. Exhibitions also put KVP in front of several utilities at once. The drawbacks are high stand and travel costs and the need to release skilled staff from the $1,200,000 testing line while absenteeism is already 8% and agency cover costs $230 a day. Attendance does not guarantee that the right procurement officers stop by.

Direct mail to procurement teams: A targeted pack containing a pressure-test certificate, delivery schedule and price can be sent to named utility buyers. It is cheap per contact, measurable through replies, and can address the 44% who have delayed orders by offering a firm delivery promise. Response rates are usually low, so KVP would need a large, accurate list, and a mailing alone cannot answer technical questions as well as a meeting.

Recommendation: KVP should choose direct mail. It targets the exact procurement officers who require certificates, lets KVP answer the 44% delivery concern in writing, and costs far less than an exhibition stand while the $700,000 loan is being repaid. Trade-directory advertising is rejected as too passive to prove certification; the exhibition is rejected because it is expensive and pulls staff from the testing line at a time when 12 of 120 workers are already absent. KVP should follow up replies with technical calls.

mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Compares at least two methods with applied reference to KVP's survey, delivery time and staffing, showing some judgement.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Evaluates all three methods in KVP's context and justifies direct mail while explaining why directories and exhibitions are rejected.

questions.question_text: KVP's absenteeism is 8% and the defect rate on cast bodies is 3.1%. Explain two benefits for KVP of its flat structure and democratic leadership.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: A flat structure shortens the chain of command, so foundry workers can report a casting fault directly to Danica Kelvin without several management layers. That helps KVP attack the 3.1% defect rate on cast bodies quickly rather than producing 25,000 units with faults before someone notices, protecting output of 100,000 units and the $1,200,000 investment in testing.

Point 2: Democratic leadership consults the 120 employees, including the 12 of 120 who are absent, about shifts and workloads. Involvement raises job satisfaction and reduces the 8% absenteeism, cutting reliance on agency cover at $230 a day. Employees closest to the valves can suggest delivery improvements, helping answer the 44% of surveyed officers who delayed orders because of the 8.2-day lead time, while keeping the $450,000 fixed costs covered. Because the testing line completes 25,000 units a month, a fault reported early by a foundry worker can be corrected before a whole batch is spoiled, saving re-testing and rework.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid point identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual explanation and analysis applied to KVP.

questions.question_text: KVP wants to cut the 3.1% defect rate on cast bodies. Consider quality circles or end-of-line inspection. Which should KVP choose? Justify your decision.
questions.model_answer:
Quality circles: Small groups of foundry and testing workers meet regularly to identify the causes of casting defects and propose fixes. This prevents faults at source, which is valuable when the defect rate is 3.1% and 61% of utility buyers require a pressure-test certificate. Repair costs and the 8.2-day delivery time fall as fewer valves are scrapped or reworked. Circles also use the knowledge of the workforce of 120, lifting morale and helping with 8% absenteeism. They need time and training, and suggestions take weeks to implement.

End-of-line inspection: Checking every finished valve before dispatch is simple and gives a clear pass-fail decision, reassuring buyers who need certificates. However, inspection only finds faults after the labour and materials in the 3.1% defective castings have already been spent; it does not stop them being made. With $450,000 fixed costs and a $1,200,000 testing line, inspecting rather than preventing wastes capacity, and 12 of 120 workers are already absent, so extra inspectors would add cost or slow the 8.2-day delivery further.

Decision: KVP should choose quality circles. They remove the cause of the 3.1% defect rate instead of merely sorting bad valves, which matters when 61% of buyers demand certification and 44% have delayed orders. End-of-line inspection is rejected because it detects waste after it has been created and would worsen delivery performance and staffing pressure. KVP can keep a light final check, but prevention must come first. With 25,000 units tested each month and complaints already falling from 52 to 29, stopping faults at source protects that improvement rather than merely sorting bad valves after the metal and labour have been spent.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Names quality circles and inspection with little application to KVP.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Explains benefits and drawbacks of one or both approaches using KVP's defect, certificate and absence data.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Evaluates both approaches in context, recommends quality circles and clearly rejects inspection with reasons.

questions.question_text: Calculate and explain how KVP's management can use its cost, break-even and productivity data.
questions.model_answer: Formula: Break-even output = Fixed costs ÷ Contribution per unit. Substitution: $450,000 ÷ ($20.00 − $11.00) = $450,000 ÷ $9.00 = 50,000 units. | Formula: Contribution per unit = Selling price − Variable cost per unit. Substitution: $20.00 − $11.00 = $9.00. | (iii) Four contextual uses explained.

sub_parts.model_answer: Formula: Break-even output = Fixed costs ÷ Contribution per unit. Substitution: $450,000 ÷ ($20.00 − $11.00) = $450,000 ÷ $9.00 = 50,000 units. Answer: break-even output is 50,000 units a year.
Formula: Contribution per unit = Selling price − Variable cost per unit. Substitution: $20.00 − $11.00 = $9.00. Answer: contribution per unit is $9.00.

sub_parts.question_text: Explain four ways KVP's management can use this financial data.
sub_parts.model_answer:
1. KVP can compare the 50,000-unit break-even point with 100,000 units produced, a margin of safety of 50,000 units, before adding capacity to the $1,200,000 testing line.
2. Contribution of $9.00 lets managers quote a discount to utilities: a $1.00 cut from $20.00 leaves $8.00, requiring 56,250 units to cover $450,000, so the trade-off can be calculated.
3. Break-even of 50,000 units shows how many valves must be sold before the $700,000 loan can be serviced, guiding treasury planning.
4. Unit cost of $450,000 ÷ 100,000 + $11.00 = $15.50 can be tracked monthly to monitor the 3.1% defect rate and the 8% absenteeism that raise unit labour cost.

working_marks: 1 mark for the correct formula and 1 mark for the accurate numerical answer in (i) and (ii); 1 mark per valid applied use in (iii).

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 2, evaluate KVP's liquidity by calculating the current ratio and the acid test ratio for 2024 and 2025. Has KVP's liquidity improved? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Calculations:
Current Ratio 2024 = 1.50 : 1
Current Ratio 2025 = 2.05 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2024 = 0.88 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2025 = 1.28 : 1

Detailed workings: 2024 current assets = $210,000 inventories + $260,000 trade receivables + $40,000 cash = $510,000; 2025 current assets = $230,000 + $300,000 + $85,000 = $615,000. The broader liquidity measure is $510,000 ÷ $340,000 = 1.50 in 2024 and $615,000 ÷ $300,000 = 2.05 in 2025. Excluding inventories, the stricter measure is ($510,000 − $210,000) ÷ $340,000 = $300,000 ÷ $340,000 = 0.88 in 2024 and ($615,000 − $230,000) ÷ $300,000 = $385,000 ÷ $300,000 = 1.28 in 2025.

Evaluation: KVP's liquidity has improved sharply. The broader measure rose from 1.50 to 2.05 as current liabilities fell from $340,000 to $300,000 and cash grew from $40,000 to $85,000. The stricter measure is more telling: it moved from 0.88, below the safe level of 1.0, to 1.28, so the firm no longer depends on selling cast-valve inventory to pay short-term debts. That is important while it services a $700,000 loan and funds a $1,200,000 testing line. The qualification is that trade receivables climbed from $260,000 to $300,000; with 44% of surveyed officers having delayed orders and 8.2-day delivery times, some of that balance could be slow to arrive. Inventories also grew to $230,000 while the defect rate is 3.1%, so stock quality should be checked.

Conclusion: KVP's liquidity has improved. Both measures are higher and the stricter one now exceeds 1.0, showing real rather than stock-dependent strength. Management should still chase the $300,000 of receivables to preserve the gain.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: States isolated financial figures or vague comments about liquidity with no accurate ratio calculations.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Calculates the current ratio and acid test ratio for both years with some contextual comment on the trend for KVP.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Accurate ratio calculations for both years, detailed evaluation of inventories, receivables, cash and current liabilities, and a justified conclusion on whether KVP's liquidity improved.

questions.question_text: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage for KVP of issuing pressure-test certificates with its control valves.
questions.model_answer:
Advantage: The survey found 61% of water-utility purchasing officers require a pressure-test certificate, so issuing one makes KVP eligible for more tenders and supports the $1,200,000 investment in automated testing. Certification also differentiates KVP from rivals and can justify the $20.00 selling price, helping cover $450,000 of fixed costs and 8% absenteeism.

Disadvantage: Testing each valve adds time and cost to the 100,000 units produced; with delivery already averaging 8.2 days and 44% of officers having delayed orders, extra documentation could lengthen lead times further. A failed test would also reveal the 3.1% defect rate to customers, and the skilled staff needed to sign certificates are in short supply when 12 of 120 workers are absent and cover costs $230 a day. The $1,200,000 testing line was bought partly to provide such proof, so charging for certificates could help recover that investment, but the paperwork adds duties to a stretched workforce.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid point identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual explanation and analysis applied to KVP.

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the base interest rate cut to 4.25%, the 5.8% minimum wage rise and the 11.0% rise in iron and bronze prices will affect KVP. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Interest rate cut (5.0% to 4.25%): The rate falls by 0.75 percentage points. If the $700,000 five-year loan is variable-rate, the saving is 0.75% × $700,000 = $5,250 a year (0.0075 × $700,000), useful against $450,000 fixed costs but small next to a $1,200,000 investment. If the loan is fixed, the benefit is delayed until refinancing. Lower rates could also encourage utilities to borrow, supporting the forecast 3.2% rise in capital spending.

Minimum wage increase (5.8%, from $12.80 to $13.54): Each hour rises by $13.54 − $12.80 = $0.74. KVP employs 120 workers but the insert gives no hours worked, so an annual bill cannot be invented. Productivity is 100,000 units ÷ 120 = 833.33 units per worker; maintaining that keeps the rise absorbable through the $20.00 price. With absenteeism at 8%, 12 of 120 workers absent and cover at $230 a day, any drop in productivity would magnify the wage cost.

Iron and bronze price inflation (11.0%): The insert does not decompose the $11.00 variable cost, so the only honest bound is an upper one: if all of it were metal-linked, 11.0% × $11.00 = $1.21 a unit; at 100,000 units that is $121,000 a year. Even one tenth of that, $12,100, exceeds the loan saving. It would cut the $9.00 contribution while the 3.1% defect rate already forces rework.

Conclusion: The 11.0% rise in iron and bronze prices will have the greatest impact. It falls on every valve, cannot be offset by a loan that may be fixed-rate, and directly squeezes the contribution needed to fund the testing line. The interest cut is helpful but conditional and small; the wage rise can be absorbed if productivity holds at 833.33 units per worker.
